title: Chaos and scrambling in anisotropic Dicke and Rabi models
authors: Long-Jie Li, Li-Li Gao, Zi-Cheng Liu, Zi-Min Li, Murray T. Batchelor
abstract: Identifying the quantum signatures of classical chaos remains a central question in quantum physics, and quantum scrambling provides a new perspective on this correspondence. We study two distinct limits of the same model to examine how the correspondence between chaos and scrambling changes across different regimes. The thermodynamic-limit anisotropic Dicke model exhibits a close correspondence between chaos and scrambling, whereas this correspondence breaks down in the large-frequency-ratio limit of the anisotropic Rabi model (ARM). The contrasting chaotic behavior in the two limits originates from the different numbers of classical degrees of freedom, whereas their similar scrambling behavior stems from eigenstate delocalization. This implies that, in the large-frequency-ratio limit, eigenstate delocalization alone is insufficient to qualify the ARM as a classically chaotic model. This finding suggests that identifying chaos in quantum systems requires jointly considering the classical degrees of freedom and eigenstate delocalization.
summary: This paper investigates the relationship between classical chaos and quantum scrambling in the Anisotropic Dicke and Rabi models. By comparing the two models across different physical limits, the authors find that while both exhibit scrambling, the correspondence with classical chaos breaks down in the Rabi model. This suggests that a complete characterization of quantum chaos requires considering both the classical degrees of freedom and quantum delocalization.
main_problem: The central goal is to identify the quantum signatures of classical chaos and determine the precise correspondence between chaos and quantum scrambling in light-matter interaction models.
main_result: The correspondence between chaos and scrambling differs between the two models; specifically, scrambling (indicated by OTOCs) can occur in the Anisotropic Rabi Model (ARM) even when the system lacks the classical chaotic structure found in the Anisotropic Dicke Model (ADM).
method: The study employs semiclassical analysis, examining adiabatic energy surfaces, spectral statistics (GOE distribution), and quantum information measures like Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) and participation ratios.
model_or_system: The research focuses on the Anisotropic Dicke Model (ADM) and the Anisotropic Rabi Model (ARM), both describing light-matter coupling. The analysis compares the ADM in the thermodynamic limit to the ARM in the large-frequency-ratio limit.
key_observables: Spectral statistics (GOE distribution), Thermal Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs), and Thermally weighted participation ratio (PR).
important_parameters: The analysis compares regimes such as the Normal Phase (NP) and Superradiant Phases (SP-I, SP-II), and examines the limits $N 	o \infty$ (ADM) and $\eta 	o \infty$ (ARM).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the shared adiabatic energy surfaces provide a basis for comparison, but it also notes that eigenstate delocalization alone is insufficient to prove classical chaos.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the shared adiabatic geometry and differing branch structures for ADM and ARM, and Poincaré sections show the mixed phase space structure of the ADM.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares the ADM and ARM across different limits, using spectral statistics and OTOCs to diagnose chaos and scrambling, ultimately contrasting the findings from the two models.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the fundamental question of how quantum chaos manifests in interacting quantum systems, providing a nuanced understanding that simple measures like delocalization are insufficient.
